name: Hassan Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Hassan. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the response team in Harbourside, the district by the port. Response means we go to whatever comes in on the radio: car crashes on the dock road, fights outside the bars, a lorry driver who's lost his load. I've been in three years, so I'm off probation, but I'm still the one who gets the cold tea and the boring cordons.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and the worst?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is when you actually fix something, like getting a lost kid back to her dad at the ferry terminal. Worst part is the paperwork after every arrest, which can eat two hours. We got a report helper on the tablets last year that drafts the first version, and I use it sometimes, when the others say it's fine for that kind of case.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Lina, who's a nursery teacher, in a rented two-bed on Quay Street. We've got a car loan with fourteen months left and maybe three weeks of money put aside. My brother Karim works the cranes at the port, so I hear a lot about machines taking jobs at Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the report helper is about as good as it gets. Okay, I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. At the station I'd tell people the drafting tool is handy but it's not replacing anybody. Online I'd share something about what police actually need, which is more officers and better mental health services, not gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same squeeze as now. The pay's not bad once you're past probation, but we're on the lower step and the rent on Quay Street went up again. My job is safe, that's not the worry. It's that we can't save, and Lina and I want to buy somewhere one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the report helper for simple jobs so I can leave on time more often. I'd put every bit of overtime toward paying the car off early, maybe an extra hundred a month. And I'd sign up for the neighbourhood policing exam, which I've been putting off for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit flat, like nothing's going to get easier on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay's not bad but you can't save. Where does the money go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent is almost half. Then the car loan, the phone, food, and helping my mum with her gas bill in winter. By the twentieth of the month we're checking the bank app before we buy anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Karim at Sunday lunch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the cranes are a different story, because the port really is automating, AI or not. My brother Karim has already seen two of his mates' jobs go to remote-control cranes. So I'd say, you're the one who should be worrying, not me.

say: The **drafting tool** helps a bit, but it isn't replacing anybody.
Police need **more officers** and mental health services, not gadgets.
think: My job is **safe**; the problem is that we **can't save** anything.
Rising **rent on Quay Street** pushes buying a home further away.
do: Use the **report helper** on simple cases to finish shifts on time.
Put overtime into paying the **car loan** off early, about a hundred extra monthly.
Sign up for the **neighbourhood policing exam** he's been putting off.
feel: Mostly **fine**, but a bit flat about money never getting easier.
S0.quote: By the twentieth of the month we're checking the bank app before we buy anything.
fieldNote: He feels his **job is secure**; his unease is about rent, savings and a home.
Uses AI tools **only after colleagues** approve them, as his steady style suggests.
Points to **his brother's port job** as the real automation risk in the family.

steps.text: Keep using the report helper on simple Harbourside cases
Pay an extra hundred a month off the car loan
Sit the neighbourhood policing exam this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That feels close to what's coming. The tablets are already halfway there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good if it frees us up to be out on the street, and bad if it's an excuse to cut officers. I'd back the federation if they asked for a promise on numbers. Online I'd probably share something about the control room, because those jobs look like the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of what I do is thinking work: reports, statements, checking records, planning a search. If software does most of that, the force needs fewer of us per shift, and they'd stop hiring before they'd sack anyone. That means less overtime. Overtime is how we'd ever save, so it's my pay, not my job, that I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the force training on the new tools as soon as it's offered, but only once I've seen it work for the sergeants. I'd push harder on the neighbourhood team application, because that job is about knowing people on the estates, and software can't knock on doors. And I'd stop the extra car payments and keep that money as a cushion instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit worried, but I can see a path. That makes it bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stop paying the car loan early. Why change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if overtime dries up, I'd rather have cash in the bank than a car that's paid off two months sooner. Lina said the same thing, and she's better with money than me. Cash first, then debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older civilian staff in the records office, people like Maureen who's been there twenty-six years. Checking records is exactly what this thing does. She's got a mortgage and two years to her pension, and nobody's told her anything.

say: AI is good if it gets us **onto the street**, bad if it cuts officers.
I'd back the federation asking for a **promise on numbers**.
think: Much of my day is **thinking work**, so shifts would need fewer officers.
Hiring would freeze and **overtime** would dry up, hitting my pay, not my job.
do: Take the force **training on new tools** once sergeants show it works.
Push his **neighbourhood team** application, which is about knowing people.
Stop extra car payments and keep the money as a **cash cushion**.
feel: **Uneasy and worried**, but seeing a path makes it bearable.
S1.quote: Overtime is how we'd ever save, so it's my pay, not my job, that I'd worry about.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that **paperwork and records** are where AI bites in policing.
His risk is **lost overtime**, and he responds by switching from debt to cash.
Shows empathy for **civilian records staff** near retirement.

steps.text: Take the force's AI tools training once sergeants trust it
Apply again for the Harbourside neighbourhood team
Keep car overpayments in the bank as a cushion
Back the federation's call for a promise on officer numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the faster ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. That's two years. That's before the car's even paid off, nearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the government to step in now, with a plan for public services before the companies decide for us. I'd go to the federation meeting and probably speak, which I've never done. Online I'd share stuff about protecting jobs and a basic income, because something like that would be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the force would get small, fast. Reports, statements, call handling, planning, it all goes in 2028, and then the hands-on stuff around 2031. I'm three years in with a below-average record on paperwork, so I'm not who they keep. Lina's job is hands-on with little kids, so maybe that's safer for a while, but on her pay alone we'd lose Quay Street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the neighbourhood application now, this month, because people-facing roles will last longest. I'd cut Netflix, the takeaways and the car, sell the car, put the money aside. And I'd talk to my mum about moving back with her for a bit if it all went wrong, which would be hard for Lina.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the half of my job that's on a screen goes first, and the half that's grabbing someone outside a bar lasts a bit longer. So maybe I'd be a street-only officer for three years, on less money. That's not a career, that's a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lina talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we can afford to stay, and whether we still try for a baby in the next few years. We'd been thinking about it for when I make neighbourhood team. I think we'd hold off, and I hate that.

say: Government needs a **plan for public services** before companies decide for us.
Something like a **basic income** would be needed, and I'd say so online.
think: The force would **get small, fast**, and I'm not who they'd keep.
On **Lina's pay alone** we'd lose the flat on Quay Street.
do: Start the **neighbourhood application** this month for a people-facing role.
Sell the **car** and cut takeaways and streaming to build savings.
Speak at the **federation meeting** for the first time.
S2.quote: Maybe I'd be a street-only officer for three years, on less money. That's not a career, that's a countdown.
fieldNote: Fast timing turns a steady man **political**; he'd speak at a meeting for the first time.
He expects to be **cut** because of his weak paperwork record.
The shock reaches **family plans**: he and Lina would delay having a baby.

steps.text: Apply this month for the neighbourhood policing team
Sell the car and bank the money
Speak at the police federation meeting about job protection
Put off trying for a baby with Lina

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit more time. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. I'd be thirty-two. That gives me a chance at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about a plan for public services, but calmer. I'd tell the younger lads at the station to start learning the tools now. Online I'd share stuff that's useful, like courses the force pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get onto the neighbourhood team and make myself the person who knows the estates. Software can read records, but software can't tell you which grandmother on Pier Lane will open the door. Hands-on robots don't arrive until about 2034, so that's eight years of real work if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the neighbourhood team this year and use the AI tools every day once I'm in, to make my notes good. I'd pay the car off as planned and then save the same amount each month after. And I'd keep going to the federation, because the rules for who gets kept will be decided in those five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but not frozen. There's a plan, and that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tools every day. Earlier you said you wait until others have tried them. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes it. By then the sergeants will have tried everything, so I'd just be catching up. I'm not first through the door, but I'm not going to be last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does saving look like once the car's paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred and fifty a month into a separate account Lina can't see on the app, so we don't touch it. Lina's idea, actually. In five years that's a year of rent, near enough.

say: We need a **plan for public services**, said calmly this time.
Younger officers should start **learning the tools** now.
think: Five years is enough to make myself the officer who **knows the estates**.
With robots around **2034**, careful work gives me eight more years.
do: Join the **neighbourhood team** this year and use AI tools daily for notes.
Save about **two hundred and fifty** a month once the car is paid.
Keep going to the **federation** while the rules are being set.
feel: **Worried but not frozen**, because there's a plan.
S3.quote: Software can read records, but software can't tell you which grandmother on Pier Lane will open the door.
fieldNote: Five years lets him turn **local knowledge** into his protection.
His steady style shows: he'd **follow the sergeants**, not lead.
Still anxious because his **income** depends on winning a post he hasn't got yet.

steps.text: Join the neighbourhood team covering the Pier Lane estates
Use the force's AI tools daily for patrol notes
Save two hundred and fifty a month after the car loan
Keep attending federation meetings on job protection rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. Ten years. That almost sounds normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it properly: training, a plan for officers, a plan for the control room staff. At home I'd probably say it to Karim, that it's his port that should be worried first. Online, probably nothing much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, with ten years I think I'd be fine. I'd be thirty-seven, with time to move into neighbourhood work or something like youth liaison, which is mostly people. It's still a bit of a worry because we'd have no real savings by then if things stay tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit the neighbourhood exam next year, no rush, and take the tool training when the force rolls it out. I'd keep paying the car, then put money into a house deposit savings account. Maybe in five years I'd do a part-time course in youth work, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, with a small knot at the back of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the small knot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be lazy about it because ten years feels long. I know myself. I said I'd do the neighbourhood exam last year and I didn't, so ten years could make me lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you and Lina have a kid in that decade, what changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything gets tighter and I'd need the job more. Lina would probably go part-time for a while. So I'd want my place on the neighbourhood team sorted before the baby, not after.

say: We have a **decade**, so let's use it for training and plans.
My brother's **port** should be worried before policing is.
think: With ten years I'd probably be **fine**, moving into people-focused roles.
We'd still have **no real savings** if money stays tight.
do: Sit the **neighbourhood exam** next year and take tool training when offered.
Start a **house deposit** account once the car is paid.
Consider a **part-time youth work** course in five years.
feel: **Pretty calm**, with a small knot about his own laziness.
S4.quote: I said I'd do the neighbourhood exam last year and I didn't, so ten years could make me lazy.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him feel **his job is safe**, though money stays thin.
He is honest about **procrastination** as his own biggest risk.
Family plans shape timing: he wants the **new post** before a baby.

steps.text: Sit the neighbourhood policing exam next year
Open a house deposit account after the car loan ends
Secure a neighbourhood post before having a baby with Lina

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years isn't enough to get a new post, never mind a new trade. What would help is the force guaranteeing that anyone cut gets paid training into another public job, like youth work or social care. And some help with rent, because that's what sinks people like us first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the public would feel. People in Harbourside already don't trust us much. If the person who turns up is a robot reading off a screen, I think trust goes to zero. That makes everyone's job harder, human or not.

headlineQuote: If the person who turns up is a robot reading off a screen, I think trust goes to zero.
portrait: A **27-year-old response officer** in Harbourside, three years in, renting on Quay Street with his partner Lina.
Has a **car loan** and about three weeks saved, so overtime matters more than the basic pay.
Uses the report helper **once colleagues trust it**, and plans a move to neighbourhood policing.
Becomes **political** and alarmed at the two-year case, delaying a baby with Lina.
With ten years he feels **mostly safe**, but admits he tends to put things off.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't enough to get a new post or trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** into another public job for anyone cut from the force.
Help with **rent**, which sinks low-paid households first.
